title: South Kingstown Early Voting Tops Election Day Ballots - Uprise RI
text:
South Kingstown Early Voting Tops Election Day Ballots Skip to main content     Newsletter Advertise Donate Toggle theme Account Select Town Rhode Island's Local News Leader News Local Features BillBuddy Our Reporting Games Contact Government · November 12, 2026 · 4 min read Early Voting Tops Election Day Turnout in South Kingstown
 Early ballots outnumbered Election Day ballots in South Kingstown, prompting a council debate over staffing 11 polling places versus offering longer early-voting hours.
 Adriana Vossari RI & Local Government Why This Matters South Kingstown voters cast 6,502 early ballots and 5,114 on Election Day. Council members discussed whether to combine polling locations or add evening or weekend early voting, but staff said polling places are set almost entirely by state law. No action was taken.
 South Kingstown, R.I. — South Kingstown Town Council members on Monday night debated whether the town still needs to staff all 11 of its polling places , after early voting outpaced Election Day voting in the Nov. 3 general election, according to the South Kingstown Town Council's published meeting recording . The council took no vote and gave staff no formal direction.
 The discussion followed an election summary from Town Manager James Manni. He said South Kingstown had 22,487 registered voters, and 12,722 of them voted, or 56.5 percent. Of those ballots, 6,502 were cast during early voting, 5,114 on Election Day and 1,091 by mail. There were also 89 provisional ballots, which are cast when a voter's eligibility must be confirmed before the ballot is counted.
 Manni said turnout was higher in 2024, a presidential year. He said 2022 turnout was about the same as this year, which he described as what a normal election looks like without a president on the ballot.
 The question raised 
 One council member asked how the town could advocate for running fewer locations as more residents vote early, saying "it's a lot to run 11 precincts." The member suggested a letter to the secretary of state, saying even eight locations would be easier than 11 for poll workers and management.
 A staff member answered, "That is completely out of our hands on the local level," and said the state sets those rules. Another staff member said "election procedures are almost 100% set by state law and the Board of Elections." That staff member said the council could send a resolution, and noted that other communities have obtained enabling legislation, a special act of the General Assembly, to use fewer polling places, though usually for a specific election.
 Long early lines, quiet polls 
 A town official said they had looked into the issue before the 2024 election after seeing early voters lined up outside Town Hall. In the final week of early voting, the official said, the line stretched to High Street and people waited 30 to 45 minutes. On Election Day itself, the official said, there was no line.
 Local sponsor The official said they were told polling locations depend less on population than on the town's large land area and getting voters to a convenient spot. After visiting every polling place, the official said, "It seems like we're way overstaffed at these, only because so many people are voting early now."
 Concerns about access 
 Another council member cautioned against the idea, pointing to a national trend in which eliminating polling places makes it harder for people to vote. "There's a reason why we have all these polling places," the member said, adding they were playing devil's advocate.
 A third member thanked poll volunteers and said they were open to the conversation but not yet in favor of fewer polling stations. The member said some residents, such as those near Gravelly Hill Road, already drive long distances to vote, and said they would want data on how much money could be saved. "But for vibes alone to shut down our polling stations, I'm not in favor of that," the member said.
 Longer early-voting hours 
 Several speakers favored expanding early voting instead . One participant said Rob Rock of the Secretary of State's Office told them the town's only options on its own are to do more with early voting, such as extended hours on some days or additional days, which would require more staff.
 A council member said a resident had told them he could not reach Town Hall before early voting closed in the afternoon because he leaves for work at 5 a.m. The member supported extended hours or a weekend day. Another member said they vote on Election Day because they cannot get to Town Hall during early-voting hours, and would vote early if evening hours were offered. That member said they wanted to understand the law first and were "nowhere near advocating for a resolution."
 The member who first raised the issue then clarified: "It's not my intention to change the number of precincts." Precincts are the voting districts residents are assigned to. The member said the idea was to combine locations, noting the town already pairs two districts at Matunuck and two at the Rec Center, and suggested perhaps three at the new high school. The member said very few people came to the Rec Center location and backed a Saturday or evening early-voting option. "No one was advocating for a resolution," the member said.
 What happens next 
 A staff member said that if the council wants to explore the issue further, it can direct town staff to prepare a report. No such direction was voted on Monday. At the council's Oct. 26 meeting, a town official reported 3,489 early voters to that point.
